This is a basic example, if you want a more complex example you can refer to the PostgreSQL documentation.

## Step 1: Overview of the Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
The write-ahead log, or WAL, is a file used by a database to keep track of all changes made to the database. Prior to writing any data to the main database, all changes are first written to the WAL.

## Step 2: How WAL Ensures Data Integrity
When a database makes a change, it first writes the change to the WAL and then to the main database. This means that even if the database crashes before the change is fully committed to the main database, the change is still safely stored in the WAL.

## Step 3: Recovery from a Crash
When the database is restarted after a crash, it can reapply all the changes from the WAL to the main database, thus recovering any data that was not committed before the crash.

## Step 4: Example
For example, suppose a database crashes after making a change to a record, but before writing that change to the main database. The change is recorded in the WAL. When the database is restarted, it can read the contents of the WAL and reapply the change to the main database, effectively
